title: Boolean logic: from truth values to valid inference
model: Classical two-valued propositional logic; or is inclusive and xor means exactly one operand is true.

items.prompt: A and B are both True. What are the values of (A or B) and (A xor B), in that order?
Which assignment makes A and not (B or C) True?
Set A=True and B=False. What are the values of ((not A) and B) and not (A and B), in that order?
Which assignment makes the material implication A -> B False?
A is False and the material implication A -> B is True. What does this tell you about B?
options: B can be either True or False.
B must be False because A is False.
B must be True because the implication is True.
The given truth values are inconsistent.

items.prompt: Which expression is the contrapositive of (A and B) -> C?
Which expression has the same truth value as not (A or B) for every assignment?
Which listed case is a counterexample to the claim that A -> B and B -> A are logically equivalent?
options: No truth assignment can distinguish them.

items.prompt: What must a complete truth table show to establish that A -> B and (not A) or B are logically equivalent?
options: They use the same variable letters.
Their outputs agree when A and B are both True.
Their outputs agree for every assignment of A and B.
Each expression has at least one True row.

items.prompt: The premises A -> B and A are both True. Which listed conclusion must be True?
An argument has premises A -> B and B, with conclusion A. Which assignment makes both premises True and the conclusion False?
A complete truth table has no row where all an argument's premises are True and its conclusion is False. What has been established?
options: Every premise is true in the actual world.
The conclusion is True under every assignment, even when premises are False.
The premises describe a cause of the conclusion.
The argument's form is valid; whether its premises are actually true is a separate question.
